source.title: Where Investment Goes
source.summary: Capital allocation, the riba prohibition, real estate misallocation, and the gap between Islamic finance theory and practice.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Two countries with identical savings rates can have vastly different growth outcomes depending on how capital is allocated. The financial system channels savings into investment, and its efficiency determines growth. Capital misallocation reduces TFP in developing countries by 30 to 50 percent. Islamic economics prohibits interest, which should theoretically redirect capital: equity-based financing (mudaraba, musharaka) aligns incentives and directs capital toward productive uses rather than safe borrowers with mediocre projects. But Islamic banking in practice hasn't delivered this. Most Islamic banks use murabaha, which is economically similar to conventional lending. Genuine profit-loss sharing remains rare. Meanwhile, Muslim-majority economies suffer from massive real estate misallocation and underdeveloped equity markets. The principles are sound. The implementation gap is enormous.

linkedin.post: Two countries with identical savings rates can have vastly different growth outcomes. The difference? How their financial systems allocate capital. Capital misallocation reduces productivity in developing countries by 30 to 50 percent. Islamic economics recognizes this challenge and offers a theoretical solution: ban interest-based lending that favors safe borrowers with mediocre projects. Instead, Islamic finance promotes equity-based financing through mudaraba and musharaka—structures that should align incentives and direct capital toward genuinely productive uses. But theory and practice diverge sharply. Most Islamic banks rely on murabaha, which functions economically like conventional lending. Genuine profit-loss sharing remains rare. The result? Muslim-majority economies still suffer from massive capital misallocation, particularly in real estate markets. The promise of redirected capital flows remains largely unfulfilled. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-re-4

instagram.caption: Two countries save the same percentage of their income. One grows rapidly. The other stagnates. The difference lies in how their financial systems allocate capital. Capital misallocation reduces productivity in developing countries by 30 to 50 percent. Islamic economics identified this problem centuries ago and proposed a solution: prohibit interest-based lending that rewards safe borrowers with mediocre projects. The theory is elegant. Replace debt with equity. Use mudaraba and musharaka to align investor and entrepreneur incentives. Direct capital toward genuinely productive ventures rather than the safest borrowers. But practice tells a different story. Most Islamic banks use murabaha—a structure that works exactly like conventional lending. Genuine profit-loss sharing remains rare across the industry. The gap between Islamic finance theory and reality leaves Muslim-majority economies struggling with the same capital allocation problems, including massive real estate bubbles.
